text:
What is Epidemiology?

EPIDEMIOLOGY

epi – “on, upon”
demo – “people”
ology – “study of”

Definition: Epidemiology is concerned with the distribution and determinants of health and diseases, morbidity, injuries, disability, and mortality in populations. Epidemiologic studies are applied to the control of health problems in populations (Quinlan 2025).

Scenario Exercise



Scenario: A city health department notices that one neighborhood has twice the rate of asthma ER visits in another neighborhood in the same city. This difference has been observed every year for the past three years.
Questions: Do you think this difference is mostly due to random chance—yes or no? If it’s not random, what might explain the difference?
What are we assuming if we believe those factors matter?

text:
Assumptions of Epidemiology


ASSUMPTION 1
Human disease does not occur at random
Disease frequency and distribution vary because of identifiable factors that increase or decrease risk.


ASSUMPTION 2
Determinants of disease can be identified
Causal and preventive factors can be studied through systematic investigation of populations.



Talk about distribution and determinants, and why that’s harder than it sounds at first. Use my own research in EM and Parkinson’s as examples.

text:
History of Epidemiology: Key Events









Event
Time Period
Description




Bubonic Plague Epidemics (Black Death)
1347 - 1351
One of the deadliest pandemics, causing 75–200 million deaths in Eurasia.


Development of Toxicology
16th Century
Paracelsus, “Father of Toxicology,” introduced the principle: “The dose makes the poison.”


Development of Biostatistics
18th Century
John Graunt pioneered statistical analysis, using Bills of Mortality to study disease patterns in London.


Development of Smallpox Vaccine
1796
Edward Jenner created the first vaccine by using cowpox to confer immunity to smallpox.


1918 Influenza Pandemic
1918-19
The “Spanish flu” infected a third of the global population, killing 50–100 million.


Identification of Smoking as a Cause of Cancer
1950
Landmark studies linked smoking to lung cancer, driving public health campaigns against tobacco use.


Eradication of Smallpox
1980
WHO declared smallpox eradicated, marking the success of global vaccination efforts.





You do not need to memorize these, but let’s talk about why they are important.
Talk about the demographic transition and epidemiologic transition when you discuss the history of epidemiology.

text:
Disease Distribution Patterns


01
Endemic
Disease or condition consistently present in a population

Relatively stable over time
Expected level of occurrence in a given place



02
Epidemic (Outbreak)
Disease occurrence in excess of what is normally expected

Sudden increase over a short period
Often limited to a specific region



03
Pandemic
An epidemic that spreads across multiple countries or continents

Global distribution
Affects a large proportion of the population

Specific Rates: Zooming into Subgroups
What are they?

Rates calculated for a specific subgroup, such as age, sex, or occupation

Why use them?

To understand who is most affected
To identify differences hidden in crude rates

Common examples

Age-specific death rate (ASDR)
Sex-specific disease rate

section: Why Can’t We Stop at Age-Specific Rates?
text:
Why Can’t We Stop at Age-Specific Rates?

Age-specific rates show where differences occur.
Comparing many age groups across large populations is messy.
We still want one number to compare populations.
Standardized or adjusted rates answer: What would the rate be if populations were structured the same way?

Standardized Rates Make Fair Comparisons
What are they?

Rates adjusted to account for differences in population structure, such as age

Why use them?

To compare populations fairly
To remove the effect of different age distributions

How are they created?

Apply each population’s specific rates to a common standard population.

Choose a standard population age distribution.
Use the standard proportions as weights.
Apply the weights to each population’s age-specific rates.
The result is an adjusted rate, as if the populations had the same age structure.

Measuring Disease Occurrence
Two core measures answer different epidemiologic questions:

Prevalence: How widespread are existing cases?
Incidence: How often do new cases occur?

Both can be crude or specific rates.

text:
Prevalence: The Snapshot
\[P=\frac{C}{N}\]
What is prevalence?

The proportion with a condition at a point or during a period in time
Includes existing cases
Ranges from 0% to 100%

Types of prevalence

Point prevalence: Existing cases at a point in time
Period prevalence: Anyone who was a case at any time during the period

text:
Incidence: New Cases Over Time
What is incidence?

Measures new cases only
Focuses on people at risk
Captures disease onset

Two forms of incidence

Cumulative incidence (CI): Risk, expressed as a proportion, over a time period
Incidence rate (IR): Rate of occurrence that accounts for person-time

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#cumulative-incidence
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#cumulative-incidence
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Cumulative Incidence
What it measures: The risk, or proportion, of developing a disease over a specified time period

Numerator: Number of new cases during the time period
Denominator: Population at risk at the start of the period

Key distinction from prevalence

Cumulative incidence includes new cases only and measures risk.
Prevalence includes existing cases and measures burden.

Limitation: Cumulative incidence does not adjust for people who enter late or leave early.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#example-cumulative-incidence
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#example-cumulative-incidence
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Example: Cumulative Incidence
Scenario

Flu season: Jan-Apr
100 elementary students healthy on Jan 1 and at risk
Same setting: crowded classrooms
All followed for 4 months
10 students get flu

\[CI=\frac{\text{new cases}}{\text{at risk at start}}=\frac{10}{100}=10\%\]
Interpretation: 10% developed flu during Jan-Apr.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#when-follow-up-time-matters
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#when-follow-up-time-matters
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
When Follow-Up Time Matters
When CI is not appropriate

Some people enroll late, some leave early, and absences vary.

Why CI fails here

Different follow-up time means different time exposed, or time at risk.
People do not share the same starting point or exposure window.

Use instead

Use the incidence rate based on person-time when follow-up varies.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-rate-tracks-new-cases-over-time
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-rate-tracks-new-cases-over-time
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
section: Incidence Rate Tracks New Cases Over Time
text:
Incidence Rate Tracks New Cases Over Time
\[IR=\frac{N}{PT}\]

Measures the speed of new cases
Uses person-time (PT): the total time each person is at risk and observed
Example: Person A contributes 1 year, Person B contributes 2 years, and Person C contributes 2 years, for a total of 5 person-years.
Stop counting person-time when disease occurs, a person is lost to follow-up, or the study ends.

Incidence Rate Example



New cases: 3
Total person-time: 102 person-years
\(IR=3/102=0.029\) per person-year
\(IR=2.9\) per 100 person-years

Interpretation: Over the study period, the disease occurred at a rate of 2.9 new cases per 100 person-years.
In plain language: For every 100 person-years of follow-up, about 3 new cases were observed.

text:
How Are Prevalence and Incidence Related?
Prevalence depends on:

Incidence: How many new cases occur
Duration: How long people remain cases

In a stable population, the rough rule is:
\[P\approx I\times D\]

Higher incidence leads to higher prevalence.
Longer duration, such as better survival, leads to higher prevalence.

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
section: Crude Death Rate: The Simplest Measure
text:
Crude Death Rate: The Simplest Measure
Definition

Crude death rate (CDR) equals all deaths in a time period divided by the total population.
Express CDR per 1,000 or 100,000 people.
Use the mid-year population as the reference population denominator.

\[CDR=\frac{\text{number of deaths in a given year}}{\text{reference population at mid-year}}\times100{,}000\]
Key point: CDR is a quick summary, but it is affected by age and sex structure.
Sample calculation for the United States in 2020:
\[\frac{3{,}383{,}729}{331{,}449{,}520}\times100{,}000=1{,}020\text{ per }100{,}000\]

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#specific-or-adjusted-death-rate
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#specific-or-adjusted-death-rate
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Specific or Adjusted Death Rate
Specific death rate, such as age- or sex-specific

Compare within the same subgroup.
Example: deaths per 100,000 among people age 65 and older

Adjusted or standardized death rate

Combines age-specific rates using a standard population.
Compares populations as if they had the same age structure.

Quick discussion: Two cities have the same crude death rate, but one city is older. What measure would you use next - specific or adjusted - and why?

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#cause-specific-mortality-rate
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#cause-specific-mortality-rate
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Cause-Specific Mortality Rate
Definition

Deaths from a specific cause divided by the population
Used to rank or compare leading causes of death

\[CSMR=\frac{\text{deaths from cause X}}{\text{mid-year population}}\times100{,}000\]
Sample calculation: Disease X in City A, 2023

Deaths from Disease X: 150
Mid-year population: 500,000
\(CSMR=150/500{,}000\times100{,}000=30\) deaths per 100,000

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#case-fatality-rate
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#case-fatality-rate
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Case-Fatality Rate
Definition

Deaths among diagnosed cases divided by total cases during a period
Used to measure severity: the probability of death among cases

\[CFR=\frac{\text{deaths among cases}}{\text{total cases}}\times100\%\]
Sample calculation: Disease X in City A, 2023

Diagnosed cases: 1,500
Deaths among cases: 150
\(CFR=150/1{,}500\times100\%=10\%\)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#proportional-mortality-ratio
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#proportional-mortality-ratio
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Proportional Mortality Ratio
Definition

Deaths from cause X divided by all deaths in the same period
Answers: How important is this cause among all deaths?
PMR is not a risk rate because it has no population denominator.

\[PMR=\frac{\text{deaths from cause X}}{\text{all deaths}}\times100\%\]
Sample calculation for the United States:

Heart disease deaths in 2013: 611,105
All-cause deaths in 2013: 2,596,993
\(PMR=611{,}105/2{,}596{,}993\times100\%=23.5\%\)

text:
Key Takeaways: Counts and Rates

Counts tell us how many events occurred.
Rates describe events relative to a population and often time.
A crude rate is an overall snapshot.
A specific rate describes a subgroup, such as an age or sex group.
An adjusted rate supports fair comparisons across different population structures.

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#key-takeaways-prevalence-and-incidence
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#key-takeaways-prevalence-and-incidence
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Key Takeaways: Prevalence and Incidence

Prevalence measures existing cases and burden.
Incidence measures new cases and risk.
Cumulative incidence: What proportion became cases?
Incidence rate: How fast are new cases occurring? It uses person-time.
In a stable setting, prevalence depends on incidence and duration: \(P\approx I\times D\).

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#key-takeaways-mortality
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#key-takeaways-mortality
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Key Takeaways: Mortality

CDR: Overall deaths in a population; affected by age and sex structure
CSMR: Deaths from a specific cause in the population
CFR: Deaths among cases; a measure of severity
PMR%: Share of deaths due to a cause; not a measure of risk
Use specific or adjusted death rates when populations differ in structure.

text:
Description Does Not Necessarily Seek Associations


Description examines distributions of single variables: middle, spread, shape, count, and proportion.
It supports resource management and planning.
Examples:

How many ventilators are available in Texas?
What is the average age of people living in Florida?
How much time elapses, on average, between exposure to a pathogen and the occurrence of disease symptoms?

Sometimes description does look for associations.
It may compare distributions of single variables within levels of another variable.
Examples:

Are people older, on average, in Florida or Pennsylvania?
Is symptom onset quicker, on average, for cholera or E. coli?

text:
Source and Target Populations

Source population: The population from which persons will be sampled and included in a measurement of disease frequency.

The source population of the original Framingham Heart Study included men and women aged 30 to 62 who were residents of Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1948.

Target population: The group of people about which the scientific or public-health question asks and for whom the disease-frequency information will be relevant, we hope.

Information about cardiac-disease risk factors from the Framingham Heart Study contributed to a nearly 75% decline in cardiovascular-disease mortality in most industrialized societies.


Sources: (Lash et al. 2021; Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#study-population-and-sample

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Study Population and Sample

Study population: The subset, up to a complete census, of the source population whose experience is included in a measurement of disease frequency.

In the Framingham Heart Study, not everyone eligible was invited and not everyone invited agreed. Those who were invited, agreed, and were free of prevalent cardiovascular disease constituted the study population.

Sample: A selected subset of a population. A sample may be random or nonrandom and representative or nonrepresentative.

Sources: (Lash et al. 2021; Porta 2008)

Cohorts


A cohort is a group of persons whose membership is defined permanently, or a population in which satisfying a set of defining events makes membership permanent.
The term is often used as a synonym for “sample” in a cohort study.
Every cohort member is enumerated: known or listed. This is not necessarily true of a closed population.


Source: (Lash et al. 2021)

Terminology Recap: Population Types









Term
Definition
Example




Population
A group of people during a defined time period who share characteristics or meet membership criteria.
The population of the United States.


Closed population
After the population is defined, it adds no new members and loses members only to death.
People who had a flu vaccine in 2022.


Open population
During a defined time frame, it gains members through birth or newly met criteria and/or loses members when criteria are no longer met or through loss to follow-up.
People who have the flu.

Terminology Recap: Source and Target Populations









Term
Definition
Example




Source population
The population from which persons will be sampled and included in a measurement of disease frequency.
Men and women aged 30 to 62 who lived in Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1948.


Target population
The group addressed by the scientific or public-health question and for whom the disease-frequency information will be relevant, we hope.
Industrialized societies to which Framingham findings about cardiac-disease risk factors were applied.

Terminology Recap: Study Population and Sample









Term
Definition
Example




Study population
The subset, up to a census, of the source population whose experience is included in the measurement.
Framingham invitees who agreed to participate and were free of prevalent cardiovascular disease.


Sample
A selected subset of a population; it may be random or nonrandom and representative or nonrepresentative.
Another, probably more common, term for study population.

Terminology Recap: Cohort









Term
Definition
Example




Cohort
A group whose membership is permanent once a defining set of events is satisfied. A cohort may be open or closed and is often used as a synonym for “sample” in a cohort study.
Similar to a population, except every cohort member is enumerated: known or listed.

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Describes Existing Conditions


Prevalence provides information about the presence or absence of a condition of interest, such as a disease, exposure, or characteristic, in a population.
It describes the extent to which the condition is present in a population during a given time frame.
Asking about the prevalence of diabetes means asking how many, or more likely what proportion, of people currently living in the population have diabetes.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-count
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-count
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Count


A count of people in a population with the condition of interest during a given time frame.
As few as 0 people and as many as all people can be living with the condition.
Range: 0 to infinity.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Proportion


The proportion or percentage of the population that presently has the condition of interest or presently has a history of the condition during a specified period, such as a history of cancer in the past 10 years.
Since none, some, or all population members can have the condition or a history of it, prevalence proportion ranges from 0 to 1, much like a probability.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-proportion-formula

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Proportion: Formula

\[
\text{Prevalence proportion} = \frac{\text{Count with the condition}}{\text{Living members of the population}}
\]

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Point Prevalence and Period Prevalence


Point prevalence: prevalence of a condition of interest at a single point in time.
Period prevalence: prevalence of a condition of interest over a period of time.
As the duration of the period shrinks, period prevalence converges to point prevalence.
There is no hard-and-fast rule for what window is sufficiently short to count as point prevalence.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-odds
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#prevalence-odds
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Prevalence Odds


Prevalence odds is a simple function of prevalence proportion, just as odds in general is a simple function of probability.
It is typically reported for convenience or desirable statistical properties.
Prevalence odds is prevalence proportion divided by 1 minus prevalence proportion.
Range: 0 to infinity.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

Prevalence Odds: Formula

\[
\text{Prevalence odds} = \frac{\text{Prevalence proportion}}{1 - \text{Prevalence proportion}}
\]

Incidence Describes New Occurrences


Prevalence measures how many cases are present at a moment or over a period; incidence measures how many new cases arise over a specified period.
Unlike prevalence, incidence measures occurrences or events: transitions from a condition being absent in an individual to the condition being present over a specified period.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

Incidence Proportion and Risk


Incidence proportion and “risk” are sometimes used interchangeably in epidemiology.
Risk can be ambiguous. Incidence proportion is less so.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence

Incidence Count


A count of new occurrences of a condition in a population at risk for the occurrence during a given time frame.
Range: 0 to infinity.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Proportion


The proportion of the population that experiences a new occurrence of the condition among those at risk of experiencing a new occurrence during a given time frame.
Like all proportions, it falls between 0 and 1.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-proportion-formula

title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Proportion: Formula

\[
\text{Incidence proportion} = \frac{\text{Count of new occurrences}}{\text{Population at risk}}
\]

objectID: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-rate
href: Module 02 - Epidemiologic Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence/Measures of Disease Occurrence.html#incidence-rate
title: Measures of Disease Occurrence
text:
Incidence Rate


A measure of the average intensity at which an event occurs in people’s experience over time.
For a population followed from baseline, it is the number of cases divided by the person-time at risk accumulated by the population.
Range: 0 to infinity.
Not a proportion.
The denominator is reciprocal time, usually person-time.
The numeric value depends on the selected time unit and therefore has no interpretation by itself.


Source: (Westreich 2019)

text:
Person-Time

Person-time is the amount of time observed for all people under study while they are at risk of experiencing an incident outcome.

Source: (Westreich 2019)
